render.title: Hypoxia and ETC gene expression
render.body:
When oxygen levels drop — a condition called hypoxia — the cell does not simply slow down passively. It actively reprogrammes which genes are expressed in order to survive.

The key regulator is a transcription factor called HIF-1 (Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1). Under normal oxygen levels, HIF-1 is continuously produced but also continuously degraded: an enzyme adds hydroxyl groups to it, marking it for destruction by the proteasome. When oxygen is scarce, that hydroxylation reaction cannot occur, so HIF-1 accumulates and moves into the nucleus.

Once in the nucleus, HIF-1 binds to hypoxia response elements in DNA and changes transcription in two coordinated ways:

1. It activates genes for glycolysis — the oxygen-independent pathway — so the cell can keep producing ATP from glucose without the electron transport chain.
2. It suppresses the expression of some ETC subunit genes, particularly those of Complex I. This reduces the overall rate of electron flow through the chain.

Why suppress the ETC genes? Because a partial or stalled electron transport chain is more likely to leak electrons to oxygen, forming superoxide and other reactive oxygen species (ROS). By dialling down ETC subunit production, the cell limits the amount of these harmful radicals generated under low-oxygen conditions.

In summary:
- HIF-1 is the master switch for the hypoxic response.
- It upregulates glycolytic genes to compensate for reduced oxidative phosphorylation.
- It downregulates selected ETC subunit genes to reduce ROS damage when the chain cannot run at full capacity.

This gene-expression response allows the cell to shift its energy strategy and protect itself until oxygen is restored.
render.summary: Under hypoxia, HIF-1 accumulates and reprogrammes gene expression: it activates glycolytic genes for oxygen-independent ATP production and suppresses certain ETC subunit genes to reduce reactive oxygen species formation when the chain cannot run at full capacity.
